article.title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
article.subtitle: In Michigan, Jocelyn Benson is polling well ahead of Abdul El-Sayed. Do gaps like that tend to shrink on Election Day?

extraction.summary: Model Talk on ticket-splitting between Senate and governor races. The median statewide split has fallen from about 25 points in 1990 to 13 in 2014 and 8 in 2022, with FLIPR projecting 6 in 2026. It walks through FLIPR's largest projected splits (New Hampshire, Vermont, Alaska, Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Maine). Using midterms from 1998 to 2022, it shows that Senate and governor polling errors in the same state are correlated (same direction 68 percent of the time), which FLIPR models with a statewide error draw, but that projected splits do not narrow on Election Day: 17.3 projected versus 17.5 actual. Adding Senate polls to governor polls adds no predictive power in regression.

findings.statement: In midterms from 1998 to 2022, in states with both a Senate and governor race and at least one qualifying poll in the final three weeks, either both Democrats or both Republicans beat their polls in 68 percent of cases. FLIPR models this with a statewide error draw in each simulation affecting House, Senate and governor races in the state.

quantities.name: same-direction poll error rate, Senate vs governor

findings.evidence_quote: In 68 percent of these cases, either the two Democrats or the two Republicans overperformed their polls in both contests.

findings.statement: Projected Senate-governor ticket splits do not narrow on Election Day: across midterms from 1998 to 2022 the average split projected by final polls was 17.3 points and the actual split 17.5, with the split larger than projected in 53 percent of cases. Regression shows adding Senate polling to governor polling, or vice versa, adds no meaningful predictive power for the final outcome.

quantities.name: share with larger split than projected

findings.evidence_quote: What’s not true, though, is that ticket splits get narrower on Election Day.

findings.statement: The median gap in margin between same-state statewide contests (Senate, governor, at-large House) was about 25 points in 1990, about 13 in 2014 and 8 in 2022 (DDHQ data), and FLIPR projects about 6 in 2026. The median is used because individual splits can be huge, e.g. Vermont 2022.
findings.evidence_quote: Based on FLIPR’s current projections, we expect statewide ticket-splitting to decrease even further, with a median gap of just six points in 2026.

findings.statement: FLIPR uses Alaska polls that explicitly report post-RCV results as well as first-round polls. It projects first-round shares and simulates ranked-choice rounds, accounting for voters who do not rank every candidate and those who cross party lines, so a candidate projected at 47 percent in round one can still be a 96 percent favorite.
findings.evidence_quote: some Alaska polls explicitly forecast the results after RCV, and FLIPR uses these too.

findings.statement: FLIPR forecasts are rounded to one decimal place, so a displayed '100 percent' means greater than 99.95 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: Our forecasts are rounded off to one decimal place, so her chances are greater than 99.95 percent, not necessarily exactly 100.

findings.statement: FLIPR's fundamentals have no variable for a non-incumbent's ideology (e.g. El-Sayed's progressivism); for incumbents, party-loyalty scores from congressional votes capture bipartisanship, which predicts overperformance. Voter views on ideology appear to be priced into the polls instead.
findings.evidence_quote: But we don’t make any similar calculation for non-incumbents.

findings.statement: Example of large projected splits in FLIPR, October 2026: New Hampshire with Democrat Pappas winning Senate by about 10 and Republican Ayotte winning governor by about 10, a roughly 20-point split; Vermont with Balint D+32 for House and Republican Scott R+3.6 for governor at nearly 70 percent; Texas Senate D+2.9 versus governor about R+3; Iowa Senate D+1.4 versus governor D+8.4.
findings.evidence_quote: the model expects nearly 20 points of ticket splitting in New Hampshire

findings.statement: In late October 2026, FLIPR's topline had barely moved for weeks given stable polling and a dearth of new polls relative to past cycles, so most remaining uncertainty was potential polling error rather than late shifts.
findings.evidence_quote: at this point, most of the remaining uncertainty in our forecast comes down to potential polling error, not late shifts in the polls themselves.

political_insights.insight: Nationalized politics make it increasingly hard to be a blue-state Republican or red-state Democrat, though governors (Scott in Vermont, Ayotte in New Hampshire, Kansas Democrats) still buck partisanship more than senators.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Shrink candidate-specific deviations over time; keep larger deviations for governors.

references.description: DDHQ data on statewide ticket-splitting since 1990

open_questions: Variance of the statewide error component relative to race-level error.
